## Lessons, failed attempts and limits

**Lessons.** RL on small bases (a 7B dense and a 16B MoE model) did not give meaningful AIME gains, so base capacity matters; reliable verifiers are crucial; and both SFT and RL are needed, since RL alone can reward-hack on ill-posed tasks while SFT alone limits exploration.

**Failed attempts.** Process reward models: fine-grained steps are hard to define, step correctness hard to judge, and model-based versions invite reward hacking. Monte Carlo Tree Search: token generation has an enormous search space, and training a good value model is hard. The authors stress these may not be inherently unworkable.

**Limitations.** Weak structured output; no tool use; "overthinking" on simple questions; language mixing for languages other than Chinese and English; sensitivity to prompts (few-shot prompting degrades performance); and little gain over DeepSeek-V3 in software engineering because slow evaluation made RL there impractical.

The central open challenge is tasks without a reliable verifier, like writing, where model-based rewards get exploited. R1 handles these with human-annotated SFT data and only hundreds of RL steps.
